feedback: If you answered 'circle' for the top-to-bottom cut too, slice the cylinder both ways and lay the two fresh faces side by side: the parallel cut is a circle, the perpendicular (top-to-bottom) cut is a rectangle — the shape tracks the direction of the cut.

If you named the cylinder's flat end or curved outer surface, hold up the freshly cut face and note: 'this surface did not exist before the cut' — the cross-section is new, not a face the solid already had.

The pre-stated reason is the diagnostic part: a mismatch between your justification and the real cut is exactly what shows the idea shifting from 'the solid has one cross-section' to 'the shape depends on how you slice it'.
activities.intendedInsight: A cross-section is the shape where the slicing plane meets the solid, so one solid yields many cross-sections depending on how it is sliced; a cylinder is only 'a circle' when sliced parallel to its base.
learnerActions: Hold a play-doh or carrot cylinder and a plastic knife.
BEFORE cutting, predict AND justify the shape of a straight top-to-bottom slice through the middle; write or say the reason.

Cut and compare the fresh cut face to your prediction (for a true cylinder a rectangle appears, not a circle; a real carrot that tapers gives a near-trapezium, an approximation to the ideal rectangle).
Make a second cut parallel to the circular ends and check that this one does give a circle.
State in your own words why the two cuts give different shapes.
activities.title: Predict, then slice: a cylinder gives more than a circle

feedback: If you insisted the tilted cut is still a circle, overlay it on a traced circle: the cut face is longer in one direction. If the cut crossed only the curved surface it is an ellipse, not a circle; if it also clipped a flat end, it is part of an ellipse with a straight edge.

Notice the pattern: straight (orthogonal) cuts can often be solved by recognising a familiar shape, but slanted (oblique) cuts need you to reason about how the plane passes through the solid, so tackle the straight cuts first and build up to slanted ones.
On the cone, a vertical cut through the apex gives a triangle, not a circle — the same lesson that the shape depends on how the plane passes through the solid.
activities.intendedInsight: Assuming a 2-D shape extends straight up into 3-D leads to calling a slanted cut a circle; oblique cuts need more careful reasoning than straight ones, a slanted slice of a cylinder that crosses only the curved surface is an ellipse (one that also cuts an end is an ellipse cut off by a straight edge), and the slice-dependence idea transfers to other solids such as a cone.
learnerActions: After solving the parallel and perpendicular cuts, tilt the knife and cut the cylinder at a slant.
Predict first: is the slanted cut face still a circle? Name the shape you expect.
Cut, then lay the slanted cut face over a traced circle of the same cylinder to compare.

Describe how the oblique cut stretches the circle into an ellipse when the slanted plane crosses only the curved surface. If your cut also runs through a flat end, the face is part of an ellipse with a straight edge, so note which case you got.
Transfer the idea to a new solid: predict then check the cross-section of a cone sliced vertically through its apex (a triangle), to test slice-dependence on a different shape.
activities.title: Tilt the cut: straight before slanted

feedback: If you expected the shape to change along the prism, your repeated cuts parallel to the end show the same triangle each time. A constant polygonal cross-section like this is the defining feature of a prism.
Connect this to measurement: because the cross-section (the base) is the same all the way through, the volume is the area of that base multiplied by the length.
activities.intendedInsight: A prism is a constant polygonal cross-section swept along its length; this constancy (which a cylinder shares, with a circle as its cross-section) links the solid's properties to volume = area of base x height.
learnerActions: Take a triangular prism (or model one in play-doh).
Slice it parallel to its triangular end, then slice again further along its length.
Compare the cut faces: check whether the cross-section ever changes along the length.
Explain why a polygonal cross-section that never changes (for slices parallel to the end) is what makes the solid a prism, and connect this to volume as area of the end (base) times the length.
activities.title: The sweep that makes a prism

feedback: If you gave a triangular prism four faces, or missed the back edges, you were counting only what the picture shows — turn the solid over and mark each face as you count to include the hidden ones (a triangular prism has 5 faces, 9 edges, 6 vertices).
Use the solid itself, not the drawing, as your source of truth for counting.
activities.intendedInsight: Counting from the solid handled in the round includes hidden faces, edges and vertices that a 2-D drawing conceals, so property-based reasoning must override the 'look' of a diagram.
learnerActions: Hold the actual solid (triangular prism, square-based pyramid) and turn it over in your hands.
Count faces, edges and vertices, marking each face as you tally it so you do not miss hidden ones.
Compare your in-the-round count with what you would have counted from a flat 2-D picture of the same solid.
State how many elements the drawing would have hidden.
activities.title: Count faces, edges and vertices in the round
